prerequisites: Basic knowledge of the organization of production areas, their automation, and product design.

learning_outcomes.text: Students distinguish the fundamental scientific approaches of industrial handling and assembly technology. They describe handling and assembly processes, their possible equipment-based realizations up to linked assembly lines, and can explain them. They also classify general assembly principles in industrial environments and illustrate the differences under technical and economic aspects.

Students justify the choice of suitable automation degrees for solving assembly-related tasks based on the imparted skills and knowledge. They integrate appropriate planning programs and thus clarify the functioning of new assembly scenarios considering flexibility, automation, and efficiency. They also illustrate their planning results in a scientifically and technically sound manner and conduct discussions with development teams on this basis.

The completion of the module enables students to analyze assembly objects and estimate suitable assembly scenarios for them. They evaluate design measures to design or modify assemblies and individual parts for assembly and automation suitability. In planning assembly processes and assembly systems, students justify their applied planning methodology and reflect their results against the background of existing (standard) solutions.

Students are able to design assembly systems with necessary components and plan a possible assembly sequence. They carry out line balancing for linked assembly stations and use appropriate planning programs for this. They evaluate assembly objects (components and assemblies) according to handling criteria and design suitable feeding mechanisms.

Students understand handling and assembly technology as an essential part of industrial production. They evaluate scientific methods for systematic planning and design of manual to highly automated assembly systems. Based on specialist literature and their own findings, they develop new approaches (including research approaches) for integrated planning of handling and assembly systems.

syllabus_topics: Fundamental terms and relationships: handling technology, assembly technology, automation, development and manufacturing costs
Handling technology: representation of handling processes, workpiece influences on handling, states of order and ordering methods
Assembly system technology: assembly principles, manual workstations, automated assembly, linked assembly lines, human-robot collaboration

Handling and assembly-compliant component design: measures for product structure – assemblies – individual parts, design principles, reference point systems, variant formation, handling and assembly technology evaluation of components

Handling and assembly planning: planning methods, procedure, precedence graphs, cycle time determination, line balancing, resource planning, ergonomics assessment, planning tools, energy efficiency and CO2 footprint
assessment_rules: The graded assessment is a term paper of 25-30 pages. The ungraded assessment is experimental work involving 2 to 4 experimental tasks. Both are required for ECTS credit.
